item.title: From Victorian Herbal Shop to Medical Cannabis Clinics
item.ns0:encoded:
In 1849, John Boot opened a small herbal medicine business in Nottingham. Victorian Britain was an age when botanical remedies played an important role in healthcare, with plants, roots and extracts used to treat everything from digestive complaints to chronic pain. Among the medicines gaining recognition during this period was Cannabis indica, commonly known as Indian hemp.

Cannabis was no stranger to Victorian medicine. Following the pioneering work of physician William Brooke O’Shaughnessy in the 1840s, cannabis extracts and tinctures became established in British medical practice, eventually appearing in the British Pharmacopoeia in 1864.

Even Queen Victoria has a place in the story. It is frequently claimed that her physician, Sir John Russell Reynolds, prescribed cannabis to relieve her dysmenorrhoea, or painful menstruation. Although no definitive evidence has emerged that the Queen herself took cannabis, Reynolds was a recognised advocate of its medicinal properties. Writing in The Lancet in 1890, he discussed its therapeutic applications, including the relief of menstrual pain.

Meanwhile, John Boot’s modest herbal establishment was growing into what would become one of Britain’s best-known pharmacy chains. Although there is no confirmed evidence that his original shop stocked cannabis, the business was founded during an era when plant-based medicines, including cannabis, were part of the medical landscape.

Businesses often talk about reinventing themselves, but sometimes innovation is simply a return to their roots. Boots has grown from a modest Nottingham herbal shop into an international pharmacy brand, passing through different ownership structures along the way. With a further change of ownership agreed involving Canadian investors, its move into medicinal cannabis offers an intriguing historical parallel. Nearly 180 years after John Boot began selling herbal remedies, the company is once again exploring the place of plant-derived medicines in healthcare.

Now, 177 years later, Boots has launched SureLeaf, a private medical cannabis service offering specialist consultations and access to prescribed cannabis-based medicines for eligible patients.

Announced on 16 November 2026, the service marks an interesting development in the evolution of British healthcare. A company whose origins lie in Victorian herbal medicine is now participating in the modern, tightly regulated world of medicinal cannabis.

Of course, today’s medicines are subject to scientific assessment, prescribing controls and clinical oversight that would have been unimaginable in John Boot’s day. Yet the historical parallels are striking.

From the herbal preparations of Victorian Nottingham to specialist cannabis prescribing in twenty-first-century Britain, Boots’ journey reflects the changing relationship between plants, medicine and public acceptance.

Perhaps the real story isn’t that Boots is reinventing itself, but that, despite nearly two centuries of change, expansion and shifting ownership, it is finding a new expression of its original purpose. From John Boot’s Victorian herbal remedies to today’s specialist-led medicinal cannabis prescribing, the science, regulations and expectations have transformed, but the connection between plants and medicine remains. Sometimes, moving forward means rediscovering where you began.

Frequently asked questions

When was Boots the Chemist founded?

Boots was founded in Nottingham in 1849 by John Boot, who initially sold affordable herbal remedies. The business subsequently developed into one of Britain’s best-known pharmacy chains.

Was cannabis used as medicine in Victorian Britain?

Yes. Cannabis extracts and tinctures were used in British medicine during the nineteenth century. Cannabis indica, also known as Indian hemp, was included in the British Pharmacopoeia in 1864.

Did Queen Victoria use medicinal cannabis?

Queen Victoria is frequently said to have been prescribed cannabis for menstrual pain by her physician, Sir John Russell Reynolds. Although Reynolds documented the medicinal uses of cannabis, there is no conclusive historical evidence that Queen Victoria personally received or used it.

Did John Boot sell cannabis in his original herbal shop?

There is currently no confirmed documentary evidence that John Boot stocked cannabis in 1849. However, medicinal cannabis preparations were already known in Britain during this period.

What is Boots SureLeaf?

SureLeaf is a private medical cannabis service launched by Boots in November 2026. It offers specialist consultations and access to prescribed cannabis-based medicines for eligible patients, subject to clinical assessment.

Is medicinal cannabis legal in the UK?

Yes. Cannabis-based products for medicinal use have been legally available on prescription from appropriately qualified specialist clinicians since November 2018. Access remains subject to strict prescribing requirements and clinical assessment.

item.title: New cannabinoid controls:
item.ns0:encoded:
Government proposals to classify THCA, HHC and ten other cannabinoids as Class B drugs raise important questions about consumer protection, naturally occurring cannabinoids and the future of the UK hemp and CBD industries.

The UK Government is proposing changes to controlled drugs legislation that would bring twelve additional cannabinoids under Class B control, including hexahydrocannabinol (HHC) and two naturally occurring precursors of THC, tetrahydrocannabinolic acid A (THCA-A) and tetrahydrocannabinolic acid B (THCA-B).

The proposals, contained in the draft Misuse of Drugs Act 1971 (Amendment) Order 2026, follow recommendations from the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD) concerning emerging semi-synthetic cannabinoids and substances that may present risks to public health.

While the Cannabis Trades Association (CTA) recognises the importance of addressing potentially harmful substances, the proposed legislation also raises questions about how these controls will affect legitimate businesses manufacturing, processing and selling hemp-derived products.

At the centre of the issue is a fundamental distinction: the deliberate commercialisation of highly concentrated cannabinoids and the incidental presence of naturally occurring trace quantities in otherwise lawful products are not necessarily equivalent in their purpose, use or associated risks.

What is the Government proposing?

The draft Order would specifically bring ten semi-synthetic cannabinoids and two THC precursor acids under Class B control. These include HHC, HHCP, HHCH, several hydroxylated and extended-chain HHC derivatives, 11-hydroxy-THC, THCA-A and THCA-B.

The legislation also proposes amendments to the existing definition of cannabinol derivatives, intended to address substances that may not be adequately captured by current controls. The draft was originally laid before Parliament on 14 September 2026, with a replacement version laid on 27 October 2026. It remains draft legislation and requires parliamentary approval before becoming law. Under the proposed Order, the changes would come into force 28 days after the instrument is made.

The wider instrument also addresses other emerging drugs, including certain synthetic opioids and cathinones. However, the proposed cannabinoid controls are particularly relevant to the hemp and CBD industries because of the natural occurrence of THCA in cannabis plants and its possible presence in extracts.

Understanding the difference between THCA and THC

THCA is a naturally occurring cannabinoid acid found in cannabis plants. It is a precursor to delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the principal intoxicating cannabinoid associated with cannabis. THCA itself is not generally regarded as producing the same intoxicating effects as THC in its unheated form. However, when exposed to sufficient heat, THCA can undergo a chemical process known as decarboxylation, converting it into THC. The degree of conversion depends on factors including temperature, duration of heating and processing conditions.

This distinction is important when considering products deliberately manufactured or marketed with very high concentrations of THCA. Highly concentrated THCA isolates, including products advertised with concentrations exceeding 98%, have been marketed in the UK for use in herbal teas and other preparations.

Although the presence of THCA does not automatically mean a product will deliver a particular amount of THC, its capacity to convert through heating raises legitimate questions about how concentrated products are marketed, their intended use and whether existing controls adequately address potential consumer risks. These considerations are materially different from those surrounding a conventional CBD product containing naturally occurring traces of THCA.

Why could the changes affect the CBD industry?

Cannabidiol (CBD) is not itself a controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971. However, CBD products derived from hemp may contain small quantities of other cannabinoids, including substances already subject to controlled-drug legislation. The Home Office has previously acknowledged the practical difficulties of producing CBD extracts entirely free from other cannabinoids. If THCA becomes a separately controlled substance, businesses will need to consider its presence alongside existing controlled cannabinoids when assessing product compliance.

This could have implications for extraction processes, laboratory testing, product specifications, imports and finished-product compliance. It is important to distinguish between a product that deliberately contains a concentrated controlled substance and one in which the same substance is present only incidentally. Classification alone does not establish that every product containing a newly controlled cannabinoid is unlawful. Existing exemptions and licensing provisions remain relevant, but their application depends on the circumstances and composition of the product.

Are the existing exempt product provisions sufficient?

Under Regulation 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, certain products containing controlled substances may qualify as exempt products. To meet the definition, a product must satisfy three conditions. It must not be designed to administer the controlled drug to a person or animal; the controlled substance must not be readily recoverable in a manner or quantity presenting a health risk; and no component part may contain more than 1 mg of the controlled drug. All three requirements must be met.

The Home Office interprets the relevant component part as the container, such as a bottle of CBD oil, rather than an individual serving. This creates an important question about how an absolute quantity limit should operate across products and materials of substantially different sizes. A 10 ml bottle of CBD oil and a large commercial container of hemp-derived material may contain the same concentration of a particular cannabinoid, but the total quantity present will differ considerably. The 1 mg provision is an absolute limit, not a concentration-based threshold. As a result, identical trace concentrations can produce different outcomes under the quantity condition depending on the amount of material held in a component part.

This does not mean that all bulk hemp materials currently qualify for exemption. Some activities involving cannabis plants, controlled plant material or non-exempt extracts already require Home Office licensing. Nevertheless, the proposed addition of THCA creates a further reason to examine whether the existing framework provides sufficient clarity and proportionality for the modern hemp and CBD supply chain.

Implications for hemp cultivation, extraction and manufacturing

The UK hemp and CBD industries encompass a wide range of activities, from cultivation and primary processing through to extraction, formulation, manufacturing, wholesale distribution and retail. Many businesses operating in these sectors already work within established licensing, security, quality assurance and testing requirements. Introducing additional controlled cannabinoids may affect how businesses assess their materials, particularly where cannabinoid profiles change through processing or naturally occurring compounds are present at trace levels.

Testing methods will be especially important. Businesses need reliable analytical techniques capable of distinguishing THCA from THC, identifying relevant controlled cannabinoids and quantifying them accurately. Without clear and consistent requirements, businesses may face additional uncertainty over product specifications, laboratory results and supply-chain documentation.

The CTA believes these practical considerations deserve attention before the changes are implemented, particularly for smaller businesses that may have limited capacity to absorb additional compliance costs.

Any assessment must also recognise that bulk operators and manufacturers are not necessarily working under the same conditions as businesses selling finished consumer products. Existing security, licensing and handling obligations should be taken into account rather than duplicated unnecessarily.

What does the proposed legislation actually exempt?

The draft Order contains an important qualification: the twelve newly listed cannabinoids are specified with an exception where they are contained in cannabis or cannabis resin. However, that wording should not be interpreted as a blanket exemption for CBD oils, extracted cannabinoids or other finished products.

Cannabis and cannabis resin are themselves controlled under existing legislation, and the status of processed extracts or consumer products depends on their legal classification, composition and any applicable exemptions. Clarification will therefore be important for businesses seeking to understand how the new provisions interact with existing requirements.

There is also a distinction between controlling the raw cannabis plant, controlling an isolated cannabinoid and assessing a finished preparation containing several cannabinoids. These are different circumstances, and the regulatory consequences should be understood accordingly.

CTA: Regulation must be guided by evidence and practical realities

Marika Graham-Woods, Chief Executive Officer of the Cannabis Trades Association, said:

“We fully recognise the need for sensible controls where products are being marketed in ways that may present risks to consumers. If gaps in the existing legislation are being exploited, it is reasonable for the Government to address them.
“However, we must be careful not to create unintended consequences for the legitimate hemp and CBD industries. There is a considerable difference between selling a highly concentrated THCA isolate and a CBD product containing naturally occurring trace amounts of THCA.
“Our members already operate within a demanding regulatory environment, and any additional controls need to be proportionate, practical and supported by clear guidance, science and a clear view to consumer risk.
“Good regulation should protect consumers without placing unnecessary burdens on responsible businesses. We would welcome the opportunity to work with the Home Office to ensure that balance is achieved.”

The importance of assessing industry impact

The explanatory note accompanying the draft Order states that a full impact assessment has not been produced because no significant impact on the private, voluntary or public sectors is foreseen. For the hemp and CBD industries, this raises a reasonable question about how potential commercial effects have been considered.

The classification of an additional naturally occurring cannabinoid could have consequences for analytical testing, quality control, product development, supply-chain operations and regulatory compliance. The scale of those effects remains uncertain, and further engagement with affected businesses would help establish whether additional costs or operational changes are likely. An assessment informed by industry experience would also help distinguish genuine regulatory risks from circumstances where existing controls already provide appropriate safeguards.

A proportionate way forward

The CTA recognises that cannabinoid regulation must respond to emerging substances, developments in product formulation and evidence of potential harm. At the same time, the legal treatment of concentrated products intended to exploit the intoxicating potential of cannabinoids should not be confused with the incidental presence of naturally occurring substances in legitimate hemp-derived products. For the UK CBD and hemp industries, the immediate priority is clarity.

Businesses need to understand how the proposed classification will affect existing exemptions, what analytical evidence will be expected and whether current licensing arrangements remain appropriate for their activities. The CTA welcomes continued engagement with the Home Office and other relevant authorities to ensure the proposed measures achieve their intended public health objectives without creating avoidable uncertainty for responsible operators. The objective should be a regulatory framework that addresses genuine consumer risks, reflects the science of cannabinoids and allows legitimate businesses to operate with confidence.

The CTA will continue to monitor the progress of the draft Order and its implications for members across the hemp, CBD and medicinal cannabis sectors.

Frequently asked questions

Is THCA becoming illegal in the UK?

The Government proposes to classify THCA-A and THCA-B as Class B controlled drugs. As at 30 October 2026, the legislation remains in draft form. The legal position of individual products will depend on the final legislation and any applicable exemptions or licensing provisions.

Is HHC a controlled drug in the UK?

HHC is among the substances specifically named in the proposed Class B controls. The proposals aim to address emerging semi-synthetic cannabinoids and update existing legal definitions.

Will CBD become a controlled drug?

No. CBD itself is not being reclassified as a controlled drug by these proposals. However, CBD products may contain other cannabinoids that are controlled. Their legal status depends on their composition and whether they meet the relevant exemption requirements.

What is the 1 mg exempt product rule?

Under Regulation 2 of the Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, a product may qualify for exemption if it meets three conditions, including that no component part contains more than 1 mg of each controlled drug. Home Office guidance interprets the relevant component part as the container rather than the individual serving.

How could the changes affect UK hemp businesses?

Businesses may need to review their testing, manufacturing, product specifications and compliance procedures where naturally occurring THCA is present. The precise implications will depend on the final legislation and the business's existing licensing arrangements.

UK Government. Replacement draft statutory instrument laid before Parliament on 27 October 2026. Contains the proposed Class B classification of THCA-A, THCA-B, HHC and nine other cannabinoids. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukdsi/2026/9780348288254

2. Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs (ACMD): Semi-synthetic cannabinoids related to tetrahydrocannabinol and cannabidiol

Published May 2025. Scientific and regulatory assessment of emerging semi-synthetic cannabinoids and associated risks, including recommendations for legislative controls. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/semi-synthetic-cannabinoids-related-to-tetrahydro-cannabinol-and-cannabidiol

3. Home Office: Drug licensing factsheet, cannabis, CBD and other cannabinoids

Updated 3 October 2024. Explains the legal treatment of CBD, controlled cannabinoids, licensing requirements and the exempt product provisions. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/cannabis-cbd-and-other-cannabinoids-drug-licensing-factsheet/drug-licensing-factsheet-cannabis-cbd-and-other-cannabinoids

4. The Misuse of Drugs Regulations 2001, Regulation 2: Interpretation and exempt products

The statutory definition of an exempt product, including the three conditions and the 1 mg per component-part requirement. https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2001/3998/regulation/2

5. Home Office: Further response to the ACMD on semi-synthetic cannabinoids

Ministerial correspondence dated 11 May 2026, addressing the Government's position on controlling THCA, including concerns raised about the potential implications for CBD, hemp and consumer products. https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/semi-synthetic-cannabinoids-related-to-tetrahydro-cannabinol-and-cannabidiol/further-response-letter-from-sarah-jones-mp-to-the-acmd-accessible

item.title: Regulatory failure. Political cover. CBD industry betrayed.
item.ns0:encoded:
Now the UK Government’s pursuit of an SPS agreement with the European Union threatens to leave British businesses paying for a regulatory failure they did not create.

The UK Government has committed to a new direction for food and agricultural regulation through its Sanitary and Phytosanitary (SPS) agreement with the EU.

For the CBD industry, this is not simply about smoother trade. It raises a far more uncomfortable question: how can the Government change the regulatory framework before its own authorities have finished the job?

Six years. No final authorisations.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) required CBD businesses to invest in scientific dossiers, toxicological studies, product testing and extensive compliance procedures.

Industry complied, often at considerable expense.

Yet more than six years later, the authorisation process remains unfinished.

Marika Graham-Woods, CEO and Chairman of the Cannabis Trades Association (CTA), recently highlighted that 10,374 validated CBD entries remained on the FSA Public List, while only six high-purity CBD dossiers had passed or received positive safety assessments. Just three had progressed towards ministerial consideration, with none receiving final authorisation.

These figures expose an extraordinary imbalance between the obligations imposed on industry and the outcomes delivered by regulators.

The SPS agreement compounds the failure

The agreement introduces dynamic alignment with relevant EU legislation, including novel foods and food supplements.

Under the intended arrangements, EU authorisations would apply in Great Britain, while existing domestic authorisations would cease to apply unless exceptions were secured.

For CBD businesses, this raises fundamental questions about the status of existing applications, recognition of scientific evidence, continued market access and the potential cost of entering another regulatory process.

The UK would also be required to follow relevant future EU rules without the voting rights of an EU Member State.

Regulatory control is being traded away before domestic regulatory obligations have been fulfilled.

The CTA has consistently advocated mutual recognition and scientifically justified equivalence rather than automatic dynamic alignment.

Removing trade barriers should not mean sacrificing regulatory accountability.

Who pays for regulatory failure?

Businesses have invested substantial sums because the Government required them to follow a particular authorisation pathway.

Those investments cannot simply be written off because political priorities have changed.

For smaller companies, further delays, duplicated assessments or uncertain market access could threaten commercial viability.

Meanwhile, the Government promotes the SPS agreement as an economic opportunity without adequately explaining what happens to businesses caught between the two regulatory systems.

The FSA did not negotiate the agreement. Ministers did.

But the Agency remains accountable for the administration of the unfinished CBD authorisation process, just as Government remains responsible for the consequences of changing it.

Neither can reasonably use the other’s decisions to avoid scrutiny.

Political expediency is not accountability

Marika Graham-Woods recently challenged the tendency for political developments to become convenient explanations for unresolved regulatory responsibilities.

Political change is legitimate. Avoiding accountability is not.

That distinction matters.

The CTA is not arguing against international cooperation or rigorous scientific assessment. It is challenging a system in which businesses are expected to comply indefinitely while those responsible for regulatory decisions face little apparent consequence for prolonged delays.

The Government must explain what protections have been secured for existing CBD applicants, whether their scientific investment will be recognised and how continuity of lawful market access will be maintained.

It must also account for the wider implications for industrial hemp, ensuring agricultural alignment does not undermine legitimate cultivation and processing.

The Government must answer for its decisions

The CBD industry followed the rules. It invested in compliance and waited for the promised regulatory decisions.

Now the Government has chosen a different direction before completing the process it established.

The SPS agreement cannot erase six years of responsibility or transfer the cost of unfinished regulation onto compliant businesses.

As Marika Graham-Woods concluded:

Political expediency must never become an excuse for regulatory failure.

Originally published by the Cannabis Trades Association.

item.title: UK Budget 2026: Regulatory reform and cannabis industry growth?
item.ns0:encoded:
Budget 2026 puts regulatory efficiency at the heart of economic growth, but will reform reach the cannabis and hemp sectors?

Chancellor John Healey's first Budget sets out plans to reduce regulatory burdens, accelerate innovation and improve accountability across government. The Cannabis Trades Association examines what these commitments could mean for CBD novel foods, medicinal cannabis and industrial hemp, and whether they could lead to more efficient regulatory processes.

Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey MP has placed regulatory reform firmly within the Government's economic growth strategy, announcing measures intended to reduce unnecessary bureaucracy, improve administrative efficiency and create a more favourable environment for business investment and innovation.

Delivering his first Budget on 28 October 2026, Healey outlined plans to remove regulatory burdens and tariffs worth almost £800 million annually to businesses, establish a new Better Regulation Executive and introduce legislation enabling innovative products and technologies to be tested and developed more rapidly under appropriate safeguards.

For businesses operating in the UK's cannabis and hemp sectors, these announcements raise important questions about whether the Government's commitment to regulatory reform will extend to the agencies responsible for scientific assessment, licensing and market authorisation.

Although the Budget contains no specific commitments to reform cannabidiol (CBD), medicinal cannabis or industrial hemp regulation, its wider objectives could provide an opportunity to examine longstanding concerns about regulatory complexity, administrative delays and commercial uncertainty.

The Cannabis Trades Association (CTA) believes that proportionate regulation and efficient decision-making are essential to creating an environment in which responsible businesses can invest, innovate and grow while maintaining high standards of consumer protection.

Regulatory efficiency becomes a government priority

The Chancellor's proposals represent a significant acknowledgement that regulatory processes can impose substantial costs on businesses and influence the UK's attractiveness as a destination for investment.

The published Budget confirms the Government's existing commitment to reducing the administrative costs of regulation for businesses by 25% by the end of this Parliament. HM Treasury estimates that achieving this target would generate annual savings of £5.6 billion and release approximately 280 million working hours for more productive economic activity.

The Treasury also identifies up to £640 million in potential additional annual gross administrative savings from further regulatory reforms detailed in the Budget.

These commitments are particularly relevant because the Government has explicitly associated proportionate regulation with faster and more predictable decision-making.

For highly regulated industries, commercial uncertainty can arise not only from the requirements themselves but also from how those requirements are interpreted, administered and enforced. Businesses must be able to understand the evidence expected of them, the processes they are required to follow and the likely timescales for regulatory decisions.

Where these processes are unnecessarily complex or unpredictable, the resulting costs can extend beyond administrative expenditure to affect investment decisions, research programmes, employment and commercial development.

The CTA considers that a credible regulatory reform programme must therefore examine both the rules governing businesses and the efficiency with which regulatory authorities discharge their statutory responsibilities.

Better Regulation Executive to oversee reform

One of the Budget's most significant announcements is the establishment of a Better Regulation Executive (BRE), a new joint unit between HM Treasury and the Office of the Prime Minister and Cabinet.

The Executive will provide direction and drive implementation of the Government's vision for a more streamlined and proportionate regulatory system that supports investment, innovation and economic growth.

Its work will be overseen by a ministerial group including the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the First Secretary of State and the Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade.

The establishment of a centrally coordinated body is potentially important because regulatory inefficiencies are not always confined to individual agencies or departments. In complex industries, businesses frequently encounter overlapping responsibilities, different administrative processes and requirements that operate across several regulatory frameworks.

The cannabis and hemp sectors provide examples of this complexity. Depending on the nature of their activities, businesses may need to engage with the Food Standards Agency (FSA), the Advisory Committee on Novel Foods and Processes (ACNFP), the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), the Home Office and the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (DEFRA).

These authorities have distinct statutory responsibilities, and their respective requirements serve different public policy objectives. Nevertheless, there are legitimate questions about whether greater coordination, clearer guidance and more consistent administrative practices could reduce unnecessary costs without weakening regulatory safeguards.

The Better Regulation Executive may provide a mechanism through which such cross-government issues can be examined, although its specific engagement arrangements and approach to individual sectors have yet to be established.

CBD novel foods: Scientific rigour and administrative efficiency

The UK's CBD novel foods authorisation framework remains an important example of the relationship between regulatory scrutiny, commercial certainty and business investment.

Companies seeking authorisation have been required to compile substantial scientific evidence, technical documentation and supporting data to demonstrate the safety of their products. These requirements are fundamental to consumer protection, and the CTA continues to support robust, evidence-based assessments.

However, scientific rigour should not be confused with administrative complexity, nor should the need for thorough safety assessments prevent legitimate examination of regulatory efficiency.

Where applications contain unresolved toxicological questions, insufficient evidence or other substantive safety concerns, further scrutiny is necessary. Equally, businesses that have invested in meeting regulatory requirements should be able to expect clear communication, transparent procedures and decisions delivered within reasonable timescales.

The FSA Board's consideration of the first CBD novel food authorisations in September 2026 represented an important milestone in the development of the UK's regulatory framework. Nevertheless, the wider authorisation programme continues to raise questions about the predictability of the assessment process and the commercial implications of lengthy regulatory procedures.

The Government's Budget commitments create an opportunity to examine whether existing processes are adequately resourced, whether avoidable administrative duplication can be reduced and whether greater transparency could improve confidence in the regulatory system.

The objective should not be to accelerate approvals at the expense of safety, but to ensure that scientific assessment and administrative decision-making are both rigorous and efficient.

For responsible CBD businesses, regulatory certainty is fundamental to investment, product development and long-term commercial planning.

Medicinal cannabis and the UK's life sciences ambitions

The Chancellor's Budget also reinforces the Government's ambition to strengthen the UK's position in life sciences, highlighting more than £1 billion in new private-sector investment and the potential for further growth in pharmaceutical innovation.

Although these announcements are not specifically directed towards medicinal cannabis, they provide a wider economic context in which the regulatory environment for cannabinoid research and pharmaceutical development should be considered.

The UK possesses significant scientific expertise and research capabilities relevant to the development of cannabinoid-based medicines. Opportunities exist across pharmaceutical formulation, clinical research, advanced manufacturing and the development of new therapeutic products.

However, the ability to attract and retain investment depends not only on scientific expertise and commercial opportunity, but also on the predictability of the regulatory environment.

Businesses involved in medicinal cannabis may encounter multiple requirements relating to controlled substances, medicines development, clinical trials, manufacturing and international supply chains. These obligations are necessary to safeguard patients, maintain product quality and ensure compliance with domestic and international law.

Nevertheless, the coordination and administration of these requirements can influence the speed and cost of legitimate research and commercial development.

The Government's commitment to supporting innovation therefore provides a basis for examining whether existing regulatory arrangements offer sufficiently clear and proportionate pathways for the development of cannabinoid-based medicines.

For the CTA, the central issue is whether the UK's ambitions for life sciences investment are supported by a regulatory system capable of responding efficiently to emerging technologies and scientific advances.

Industrial hemp and opportunities for sustainable economic development

Industrial hemp also has potential relevance to the Government's wider economic and regulatory reform agenda.

Its applications extend across agriculture, construction materials, textiles, manufacturing and other developing industries. These markets offer opportunities for agricultural diversification, domestic processing, supply-chain development and the commercialisation of innovative materials.

However, industrial hemp businesses must operate within a regulatory environment shaped by cultivation licensing, controlled-substance legislation and the requirements applicable to different plant components and finished products.

The resulting complexity can influence investment decisions and create additional costs for businesses seeking to develop new applications and commercial markets.

The Budget includes proposals to explore more efficient approaches to environmental regulation and the management of rural land and natural resources, with the stated intention of reducing administrative burdens while maintaining appropriate protections.

Although the Government has not announced specific changes to industrial hemp regulation, these proposals provide an opportunity to consider whether existing arrangements appropriately reflect the nature and risks of legitimate industrial hemp activities.

The CTA believes that regulatory proportionality is particularly important in ensuring that industrial hemp is assessed according to its agricultural and commercial applications rather than being unnecessarily constrained by frameworks designed for different uses of cannabis.

New legislation could create opportunities for regulatory innovation

The proposed Regulation for Growth Bill represents another significant element of the Budget's regulatory reform programme.

The legislation is intended to establish new powers allowing businesses to test, refine and scale innovative products and approaches more rapidly while maintaining appropriate safeguards.

Under the proposed arrangements, existing regulatory requirements could be temporarily adapted to facilitate supervised trials of new technologies or approaches. Where such trials demonstrate that an alternative approach is safe and effective, the legislation could provide a route towards permanent regulatory change.

The Government has identified a developing range of potential applications, including new technologies, licensing arrangements and environmental regulation. In his Budget speech, the Chancellor also referred to the potential for innovative medicines to be tested and scaled more rapidly.

For the cannabis and hemp sectors, these proposals raise questions about whether carefully controlled regulatory trials, alternative assessment methods or more adaptable pathways might eventually support responsible product development.

However, the Budget does not establish that CBD novel foods, cannabinoid medicines or industrial hemp activities will qualify for these arrangements. Their relevance will depend on the detailed legislation, the scope of the powers and the safeguards established for participating businesses and regulatory authorities.

The CTA will examine these developments as further details emerge, particularly where they may support innovation without compromising scientific standards or consumer protection.

Regulatory accountability must be part of the solution

The Government's commitment to reducing administrative burdens is welcome, but the success of regulatory reform should not be measured solely through financial savings or the removal of individual requirements.

For businesses, meaningful improvement depends on whether regulatory processes become more transparent, consistent and predictable.

This includes ensuring that regulatory authorities have the expertise and resources necessary to undertake robust assessments, communicate clearly with applicants and distinguish between delays arising from legitimate scientific concerns and those attributable to avoidable administrative obstacles.

The Government's response to the Small Business Regulation Taskforce, published on 26 October 2026, reinforces this direction. The response addresses the need for simpler regulatory submissions, clearer guidance, improved business support and more proportionate approaches to the design and enforcement of regulation.

Together with the Budget announcements, these measures suggest that regulatory efficiency and administrative performance will receive greater attention as part of the Government's wider economic strategy.

For industries operating within complex regulatory environments, this presents an opportunity to raise evidence-based concerns about processes that may be unnecessarily costly, duplicative or difficult to navigate.

Businesses are rightly required to demonstrate compliance with demanding legal and scientific standards. In return, they should be able to expect regulatory systems that are adequately resourced, transparent in their requirements and accountable for delivering decisions efficiently.

Regulatory accountability should therefore be considered an essential part of effective consumer protection rather than a competing objective.

What the Budget means for the CTA and its members

For the Cannabis Trades Association, the Budget provides an opportunity to engage with the Government on how its wider regulatory reform commitments should apply to the cannabis and hemp sectors.

The establishment of the Better Regulation Executive is particularly relevant because it introduces a centrally coordinated approach to addressing regulatory burdens and improving the relationship between regulation, investment and economic growth.

The CTA will consider how evidence from its members can contribute to discussions about administrative costs, regulatory certainty, overlapping responsibilities and opportunities for more proportionate processes.

This engagement will recognise the different regulatory requirements governing CBD consumer products, medicinal cannabis and industrial hemp, while identifying common issues that may benefit from greater coordination and transparency.

The Association will also monitor the development of the Regulation for Growth Bill and assess whether its proposed mechanisms could provide opportunities for responsible innovation within relevant sectors.

The CTA's position remains that strong regulation is essential to protecting consumers, supporting legitimate businesses and building confidence in developing markets. However, effective regulation must also be capable of delivering clear requirements, scientifically credible assessments and timely, transparent decisions.

The Government has now explicitly recognised that regulatory burdens can influence investment, productivity and economic growth. Translating that recognition into practical improvements will require cooperation between departments, regulators, businesses and representative organisations.

For the UK's cannabis and hemp sectors, the measure of success will not simply be how many regulations are removed, but whether the Government delivers a regulatory environment that is proportionate, scientifically robust, commercially predictable and accountable.

The Chancellor has set out the ambition. The next challenge is ensuring that regulatory performance reflects it.

Sources and further reading

HM Treasury, Budget 2026, 28 October 2026
https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/budget-2026-document/budget-2026-html

HM Treasury, Budget 2026: Breathing space for today, hope for the future, 28 October 2026
https://www.gov.uk/government/news/budget-2026-breathing-space-for-today-hope-for-the-future

UK Parliament, Government response to the Small Business Regulation Taskforce, 26 October 2026
https://questions-statements.parliament.uk/written-statements/detail/2026-10-26/hcws416

Frequently asked questions

Does the UK Budget 2026 introduce changes to cannabis and hemp regulations?

No specific changes to CBD, medicinal cannabis or industrial hemp legislation were announced in the October 2026 Budget. However, the Government's wider commitment to reducing regulatory burdens, improving efficiency and supporting innovation could create opportunities for future reform. Any changes affecting these sectors would require further policy development and, where necessary, legislative action.

What is the Better Regulation Executive and why does it matter?

The Better Regulation Executive is a new cross-government body announced in Budget 2026 to improve regulatory efficiency, reduce unnecessary bureaucracy and support economic growth. For cannabis and hemp businesses, it could provide an opportunity to address overlapping regulatory responsibilities, administrative delays and inconsistent guidance across government departments and agencies.

Could regulatory reform speed up CBD novel food authorisations?

The Government's commitment to more efficient regulation could provide an opportunity to review administrative processes within the UK's CBD novel foods authorisation system. However, the Budget does not announce accelerated CBD approvals or changes to scientific safety requirements. The Cannabis Trades Association supports maintaining rigorous safety assessments while improving transparency, communication and decision-making timescales.

What could Budget 2026 mean for medicinal cannabis businesses?

The Budget reinforces the Government's ambition to encourage life sciences investment and pharmaceutical innovation. Although medicinal cannabis is not specifically identified for regulatory reform, improvements to research licensing, administrative coordination and regulatory predictability could support legitimate cannabinoid research and medicines development. Existing controlled-drug and medicines legislation remains applicable.

How could regulatory reform benefit the UK industrial hemp industry?

Industrial hemp businesses could benefit from clearer licensing procedures, better coordination between government departments and more proportionate regulation of agricultural and commercial activities. Hemp has applications in construction, textiles, manufacturing and sustainable agriculture. However, the Budget does not introduce specific changes to hemp cultivation licences or controlled-substance requirements.

What is the proposed Regulation for Growth Bill?

The proposed Regulation for Growth Bill is intended to create opportunities for businesses to test and develop innovative products, technologies and processes under appropriate regulatory safeguards. This could include supervised trials in which certain requirements are temporarily adapted. Whether CBD products, medicinal cannabis or industrial hemp businesses could participate will depend on the final legislation and eligibility criteria.

item.title: CTA contributes to United Nations review of international drug policy
item.ns0:encoded:
The Cannabis Trades Association (CTA) has submitted its recommendations to a United Nations independent expert panel reviewing the international drug-control system, calling for evidence-based regulation that protects public health while supporting legitimate medicine, scientific research and industrial hemp.

The independent expert panel, established under Resolution 68/6 of the United Nations Commission on Narcotic Drugs (CND), is examining the effectiveness of the international drug-control framework and identifying opportunities for improvement. The review provides an opportunity to consider whether existing policies are delivering meaningful outcomes for public health, patient access, scientific progress and legitimate economic activity.

Why international drug policy needs to evolve

The international drug-control system is founded on three principal conventions adopted in 1961, 1971 and 1988. Together, they establish obligations intended to prevent illicit trafficking, protect public health and ensure the availability of controlled substances for legitimate medical and scientific purposes. However, the CTA's submission highlights how inconsistent national interpretations and disproportionate regulatory requirements can create unnecessary barriers without corresponding public-health benefits.

The Association argues that effective regulation must distinguish between illicit drug activity, prescribed medicines, non-intoxicating cannabinoid products and legitimate agricultural production. Applying equivalent restrictions to activities presenting substantially different risks can undermine the objectives that international drug policy is intended to achieve.

Medicinal cannabis, industrial hemp and regulatory consistency

Drawing on its regulatory engagement in the United Kingdom and internationally, the CTA identified several areas requiring greater clarity and cooperation. For medicinal cannabis, the submission highlights barriers involving treatment costs, professional understanding, international travel and continuity of lawful treatment. Although specialist prescribing became legal in the UK in November 2018, patients continue to encounter practical difficulties accessing treatment.

Industrial hemp presents different challenges. Despite its established agricultural and commercial applications, inconsistent national approaches to low-THC crops, flowers, leaves and extracts can restrict legitimate cultivation, processing and trade. The CTA emphasised the importance of distinguishing international treaty obligations from additional restrictions imposed through domestic agricultural, medicines, food and controlled-drug legislation, while also calling for improvements to scientific research licensing and international regulatory cooperation.

Regulation must deliver meaningful outcomes

Marika Graham-Woods, Chief Executive Officer and Chair of the Cannabis Trades Association, emphasised the importance of practical reform and the need to assess international drug policy against measurable outcomes rather than the extent of regulatory restriction.

"International drug policy must be judged by what it achieves, not simply by what it restricts. We need a framework that protects public health, prevents illicit activity and enables legitimate medicine, research and agriculture to flourish. These objectives are not mutually exclusive. The CTA's contribution calls for practical, evidence-based reforms that deliver meaningful outcomes for patients, responsible businesses and society."

Seven recommendations for meaningful reform

The CTA's submission identifies seven priorities for the Expert Panel's consideration, beginning with greater clarity about international treaty obligations and improved access to legitimate controlled medicines. It calls for evidence-based scheduling decisions, proportionate scientific research licensing and clearer international guidance concerning industrial hemp production and trade.

Further recommendations address regulatory consistency between drug-control, medicines, food and agricultural authorities, alongside proportionate enforcement, professional training and human rights safeguards. The CTA also advocates transparent evaluation of drug policy through measurable public-health, safety and regulatory outcomes, recognising that arrests, seizures and enforcement activity alone cannot adequately demonstrate policy effectiveness.

“International drug policy must be judged by what it achieves, not simply by what it restricts. We need a framework that protects public health, prevents illicit activity and enables legitimate medicine, research and agriculture to flourish. These objectives are not mutually exclusive. The CTA's contribution calls for practical, evidence-based reforms that deliver meaningful outcomes for patients, responsible businesses and society.”

Marika Graham-Woods, CEO and Chair

Ensuring industry expertise informs international policy

The CTA welcomes the opportunity for legitimate industry stakeholders to contribute alongside healthcare professionals, researchers, patients and civil society. Practical regulatory experience can help identify where international obligations are working effectively and where their implementation creates unintended consequences, particularly for businesses and patients operating within lawful frameworks.

Through its submission, the Association continues to advocate for proportionate, scientifically informed regulation that protects society while enabling responsible development across the medicinal cannabis, CBD and industrial hemp sectors. The CTA hopes its recommendations will contribute to a more coherent international approach that maintains appropriate safeguards while recognising the importance of medical access, research, sustainable agriculture and legitimate trade.

item.title: CTA welcomes EU whole-plant hemp proposals and seeks clarity on CBD
item.ns0:encoded:
The Council of the European Union has backed proposals to bring all parts of the hemp plant within the EU’s agricultural market framework. The proposals are still under negotiation and do not themselves authorise CBD foods. The Cannabis Trades Association welcomes the development and is seeking clarity on how the proposed UK–EU SPS Agreement would affect British CBD authorisations.

A positive direction for hemp

On 19 October, the Council agreed its partial negotiating position on proposed changes to the Common Market Organisation for agricultural products, as part of the EU’s framework for 2028–2034.

The position supports harmonising hemp production and marketing rules across EU member states, with the sector covering all plant parts. Certified-seed requirements and a 0.3% THC threshold would remain, alongside safeguards protecting national policies on drugs, public health and security. The proposal still requires negotiations with the European Parliament. (consilium.europa.eu⁠)

For the CTA, this direction recognises the importance of considering hemp as a crop with multiple commercial applications. More consistent rules could support investment and supply-chain development. However, agricultural recognition should not be interpreted as unrestricted permission to use every plant part in any finished product.

CBD market access remains a separate question

The proposed UK–EU SPS Agreement creates a further issue for British CBD businesses. Although intended to reduce barriers to agrifood trade, the agreement would also involve alignment with relevant EU rules, including those governing novel foods.

The Food Standards Agency’s September board paper states that, without an agreed exception, EU authorisation would be required to market CBD novel foods in Great Britain. Businesses would apply through the EU system, and Great British authorisations would cease to apply. (gov.uk⁠)

This raises significant questions for businesses that have invested in British applications, safety evidence and regulatory compliance. Government guidance identifies mid-2027 as the intended implementation date, subject to negotiations, with detailed arrangements still being finalised. (gov.uk⁠)

Clarity needed before the November summit

The UK–EU summit in Brussels on 20 November provides an opportunity to seek answers. Agrifood rules are among the areas in which leaders will review progress. (consilium.europa.eu⁠)

Marika Graham-Woods, CEO and Chairman of the Cannabis Trades Association, said:

“Recognising the whole hemp plant within agricultural policy is a welcome step. Farmers and businesses need a framework that allows them to develop the crop’s commercial potential responsibly.
“However, recognition must be supported by workable routes to market. British CBD businesses have committed substantial time and resources to the UK regulatory process. They need to know how their applications, evidence and any authorisations will be treated under an SPS agreement.
“Ahead of the November summit, we are calling for clear answers on exceptions, transitional arrangements and continued market access. Businesses cannot plan investment and production around unresolved regulatory questions.”

The CTA supports measures that simplify trade and maintain consumer protection. It urges the UK Government to explain how those objectives will be delivered for hemp and CBD businesses, including those whose products are sold solely within Britain.

Questions answered

Has the EU approved unrestricted use of the whole hemp plant?

No. The Council has agreed a negotiating position supporting agricultural rules covering all hemp plant parts. Further negotiations are required, and safeguards for national drugs, health and public security rules remain.

Do the hemp proposals authorise CBD foods?

No. Recognising hemp within agricultural policy does not replace the separate authorisation requirements for CBD novel foods.

How could the UK–EU SPS Agreement affect British CBD businesses?

The FSA has stated that, without an agreed exception, EU novel food authorisations would replace Great British authorisations under the proposed agreement. Businesses need clarity on the treatment of existing authorisations, pending applications and transitional arrangements.

item.title: Eight years legal, but is medical cannabis understood?
item.ns0:encoded:
Eight years after cannabis-based products for medicinal use (CBPMs) became legally available on prescription in the UK, questions remain about patient access, affordability, professional understanding and public attitudes. Medical Cannabis Awareness Week (MCAW) 2026 aims to bring those issues into sharper focus, with patients at the centre of the conversation.

Running from 1 to 8 November 2026, this year's campaign adopts the theme 'Together for Patients', bringing together patient advocates, healthcare professionals, researchers and organisations working across the medical cannabis sector.

The programme comprises 22 sessions over eight days, with most activities available online and free to attend.

Eight years of legal prescribing, but challenges remain

The UK changed its legislation on 1 November 2018, allowing specialist doctors to prescribe cannabis-based products for medicinal use under defined circumstances. That change established an important legal route to treatment. However, legal recognition has not automatically translated into widespread understanding, affordable access or consistent experiences for patients.

Medical Cannabis Awareness Week highlights several challenges that continue to affect the patient community, including the affordability and availability of prescribed medicines, stigma, access to reliable information and awareness among healthcare professionals.

For patients, these issues can extend beyond obtaining a prescription. Understanding how to travel with medication, managing treatment in public spaces and explaining the legitimacy of prescribed cannabis to others can all form part of everyday life. These are not simply matters of public perception. They demonstrate the importance of clear information, appropriate professional education and a healthcare environment in which patients can discuss their treatment without unnecessary misunderstanding.

A collaborative approach to patient advocacy

First established in 2020, Medical Cannabis Awareness Week has developed into a collaborative campaign bringing different patient organisations, advocates and supporters together. The 2026 programme is principally hosted by Medicinal Cannabis UK, United Patients Alliance and PatientsCann UK.

Rather than concentrating on a single organisation or perspective, this year's campaign seeks to encourage discussion across the patient community and wider medical cannabis sector. The programme brings together personal experiences, clinical perspectives, educational sessions and opportunities for community engagement.

Importantly, the campaign also recognises that meaningful improvements in patient care require cooperation between different stakeholders, even where their views or priorities may differ.

From awareness to meaningful progress

Medical cannabis has been part of the UK's legal prescribing framework for eight years, but awareness alone cannot resolve every challenge associated with patient access. The continuing discussion must also address the practical circumstances in which patients obtain, afford, receive and use their prescribed medicines.

Greater understanding among healthcare professionals, better public information, constructive engagement with policymakers and patient involvement in future decisions all have a role to play. The theme 'Together for Patients' provides an opportunity to consider how the patient community, healthcare providers, industry and relevant authorities can work towards more consistent, informed and patient-centred approaches.

For the Cannabis Trades Association, constructive engagement between patients, professionals, regulators and responsible businesses remains an important part of developing a well-informed and appropriately regulated medical cannabis sector.

item.title: Biological Data is becoming a strategic asset in drug development
item.ns0:encoded:
Competition in biotechnology increasingly involves access to biological information as well as medicines, laboratories and manufacturing. An FT Live report, China’s biotech boom, identifies human biological data as a growing strategic concern, with implications for scientific discovery, international partnerships and security.

For the medicinal cannabis sector, this wider development raises questions about how research information is collected, shared and protected. Its value depends both on what it can reveal and on the confidence patients have in the organisations using it.

Why biological information has strategic value

The report discusses multiomic data, which combines different layers of biological information. These may include genetic sequences, gene activity, proteins and other measures that help researchers investigate how the body functions.

Analysed together, these layers can reveal patterns that would be harder to identify from a single source. They can support research into disease mechanisms and potential treatments, including approaches intended to account for differences between patients.

FT Live describes governments increasingly treating this information as a strategic asset. Access to extensive datasets may strengthen research capabilities, while control over their use carries commercial and security implications.

However, biological data is not interchangeable with all health information. A prescribing record, a patient questionnaire and a genetic dataset provide different kinds of evidence and create different practical challenges.

International collaboration brings questions about control

Research partnerships can bring together expertise, funding and analytical capabilities that one organisation could struggle to assemble independently. Sharing information may be essential to that collaboration.

The report also highlights tension between scientific openness and security priorities. Businesses need to understand where information is held, which organisations can access it and what additional uses their agreements permit.

The location of a server is only part of that picture. Access by contractors, onward sharing and the use of data in further research also deserve attention when a partnership is designed.

Removing names does not always remove identification

The UK’s Information Commissioner’s Office identifies genetic data and information concerning health as special categories of personal data requiring additional protection. item.title: Billion-Dollar Pharma Deals reveal what buyers are really paying for
item.ns0:encoded:
International pharmaceutical companies are increasingly turning to Chinese biotechnology businesses for new medicines, striking licensing agreements with potential values running into billions of dollars. An FT Live report, China’s biotech boom, examines the growth of these partnerships and the complementary strengths behind them.

For cannabis businesses seeking investment or development partners, the story offers a useful insight into what makes scientific innovation commercially attractive. It also demonstrates why the headline value of an agreement needs careful interpretation.

Why pharmaceutical companies are looking outside

Established drugmakers need new products to sustain their businesses as older medicines lose patent protection. Once exclusivity expires, competing products can put pressure on revenues, creating what the industry calls a “patent cliff”.

The FT Live report cites an Evaluate Pharma estimate that medicines generating approximately $180 billion in annual revenue will lose patent protection by 2028. That figure represents the revenues associated with those medicines, rather than a prediction that all those revenues will disappear.

This pressure helps explain the interest in externally developed treatments. A pharmaceutical company can strengthen its pipeline by securing rights to promising research from another business, rather than relying entirely on discoveries made internally.

The headline figure is not the upfront payment

GSK’s July 2025 agreements with Hengrui Pharma illustrate how these arrangements work. Covering up to 12 innovative medicines, they included $500 million in upfront fees and approximately $12 billion in potential future milestone payments, conditional on all programmes being optioned and all milestones being achieved. Royalties were additional. (gsk.com⁠)

Similarly, Argo Biopharma’s September 2025 agreements with Novartis included a $160 million upfront payment. Argo was also eligible for potential milestone and option payments of up to $5.2 billion, alongside royalties on commercial sales. (argobiopharma.com⁠)

These structures distinguish immediate funding from payments dependent on future progress. Scientific promise may attract an agreement, but much of its potential value remains tied to development and commercial success.

Partnerships combine different capabilities

FT Live describes agreements in which Chinese companies contribute early-stage research while overseas partners take responsibility for later development and commercialisation outside China.

The smaller innovator may gain funding, regulatory expertise and access to international development networks. The larger company gains access to a potential medicine or technology that complements its existing business.

For the innovator, this can provide a route to market without immediately building a complete international pharmaceutical operation. However, the scope of the rights granted and the responsibilities retained remain central to the agreement.

What cannabis developers can take from this

The report does not establish that pharmaceutical companies are seeking cannabinoid assets on comparable terms. Its relevance is the way businesses demonstrate value to prospective partners.

For a cannabinoid developer, an attractive proposition could involve a reproducible formulation, a delivery technology, specialist development knowledge or a medicine candidate supported by credible evidence. The business needs to explain what its asset contributes and what further work is required.

A partner will also need clarity about ownership, access to supporting data and the ability to reproduce results. Commercial ambition becomes more persuasive when those foundations are documented.

For CTA members pursuing medicine development, the practical question is what another organisation would gain by partnering with them. A clear answer, supported by evidence and a realistic development plan, provides a stronger basis for negotiation than comparisons with the largest deals elsewhere in pharmaceuticals.

Originally published by the Cannabis Trades Association.

item.title: Pharmaceutical Supply Security is moving beyond the lowest price
item.ns0:encoded:
The concentration of pharmaceutical research and production in a limited number of countries is prompting a wider reassessment of medicine supply security. An FT Live report, China’s biotech boom, describes an industry benefiting from international expertise while facing questions about how dependent it has become on particular providers.

For medicinal cannabis businesses, the implications extend beyond the cost of buying or producing a product. Understanding the organisations, services and infrastructure supporting its delivery is central to assessing how reliably that product can reach patients.

Expertise can become a point of dependence

FT Live describes how Chinese contractors have become embedded in international pharmaceutical development and manufacturing. Their capabilities support both established medicines and products still undergoing clinical research.

This creates a commercial advantage for companies accessing specialist expertise, but also a potential vulnerability. Replacing an important contractor may require technical work, new agreements and changes to established processes.

The report describes pharmaceutical companies reassessing their exposure to geopolitical uncertainty. Bristol Myers Squibb, for example, developed contingency plans to protect medicine supply continuity.

The broader issue is that a relationship chosen for its efficiency can become difficult to replace. Supply planning therefore needs to consider how a business would respond if access to that relationship changed.

Europe is placing greater emphasis on resilience

The report identifies the EU’s Critical Medicines Act initiative as part of a shift towards treating pharmaceutical capacity as strategic infrastructure.

In May 2026, the Council of the EU and European Parliament reached a provisional agreement intended to diversify critical medicine supply chains, strengthen European manufacturing and support coordinated procurement. The agreement included resilience-related requirements in public procurement procedures for critical medicines. (consilium.europa.eu⁠)

This illustrates a broader policy direction: availability and exposure to disruption are becoming more prominent considerations alongside price. It does not establish that medicinal cannabis products fall within those measures, but it provides context for the wider debate about dependable medicine supply.

Several suppliers can share the same vulnerability

For cannabis businesses, supplier diversity needs to be examined beyond the names on purchase orders. Two distributors may obtain products from the same manufacturer, while several producers may depend on one testing provider or transport route.

An apparently varied supplier list can therefore conceal a shared point of failure. Mapping those connections helps a business understand whether its alternatives are genuinely independent.

Contingency planning also requires practical detail. An alternative supplier is more useful when the business understands its capacity, product suitability, documentation and realistic delivery times. A name held in reserve offers limited protection if those questions remain unanswered.

Domestic production is one part of the picture

Producing closer to the intended market can reduce some dependencies, but it does not automatically secure the entire supply chain. A domestic operation may still rely on imported equipment, specialist materials, external testing or overseas technical support.

International sourcing can also provide resilience where it gives access to suitable, independently supported alternatives. The relevant question is how the complete arrangement performs under pressure.

This is especially significant when discussing investment in domestic cannabis capacity. Cultivation, processing, testing and distribution need to be considered together when assessing what a project can deliver.

Continuity matters at the patient end

A disruption becomes most consequential when it affects the availability of a prescribed medicine. Businesses need clear arrangements for identifying emerging shortages and communicating through the supply chain.

For CTA members, the report offers a reason to examine dependencies before a disruption exposes them. A well-documented supply chain, supported by workable alternatives and timely communication, can help businesses make more informed purchasing decisions and protect continuity where it matters most.

Originally published by the Cannabis Trades Association.

item.title: Speed is becoming a deciding factor in Pharmaceutical Outsourcing
item.ns0:encoded:
The competitive advantage of pharmaceutical contractors is increasingly being measured in time as well as money. An FT Live report on China’s biotech expansion describes how faster development, established technical networks and experienced specialists are influencing where companies commission research and manufacturing.

For cannabis businesses developing products or commissioning testing, the findings offer a useful perspective on how to assess external partners. The price of a service is only part of its value; reliable delivery can determine whether a project remains commercially viable.

Moving beyond the low-cost argument

In China’s biotech boom, FT Live describes China’s expanding role in outsourced pharmaceutical research and production. Contract research organisations, known as CROs, undertake research and development activities for other businesses. Contract manufacturing organisations, or CMOs, provide production capabilities.

The report attributes their development partly to investment in a skilled workforce and the accumulation of specialist knowledge. These capabilities serve both Chinese companies and international clients.

Egan Peltan, co-founder and chief executive of Stealth Biotech, explains the changing appeal: “We use them because of the efficiency and time savings.”

His account challenges the assumption that outsourcing decisions are principally about finding the cheapest provider. For some developers, access to capable teams that can complete work efficiently has become the stronger attraction.

Where time is being saved

According to McKinsey figures cited in the report, patient enrolment in Chinese clinical trials takes around half the global average time. The report also states that the cost per patient is roughly 50 per cent lower than in the US and Europe.

These comparisons measure different things. Faster recruitment can help a trial progress, while lower recruitment costs may stretch available funding. Neither figure establishes that every Chinese contractor offers the same advantage.

The report also identifies administrative delays elsewhere. Steve Ruston, chief executive of UK biotech Persica, describes hospital contracts taking months to finalise. His experience highlights how development can be slowed by the arrangements surrounding scientific work.

Delays consume more than the timetable

For a company funding development before earning revenue, waiting has a direct financial consequence. Staff, facilities and other commitments may continue to require payment while a project is unable to advance.

A delayed result can also hold up subsequent work. Formulation decisions may depend on analytical findings, while manufacturing plans may depend on completed development studies. When one stage slips, several others can follow.

This makes delivery performance commercially significant. A competitive quotation can lose its appeal if unclear requirements, poor communication or incomplete records create additional work.

The relevance to cannabis businesses

The report does not compare cannabis laboratories or recommend particular providers. Its findings nevertheless suggest useful questions for businesses commissioning testing, formulation development or specialist manufacturing.

Can the partner explain its methods and deliverables? Is the timetable realistic? Will the documentation support the next stage of the project? How will unexpected findings or delays be communicated?

For example, cannabinoid testing is more useful when a business understands what was measured, how it was measured and whether the method suits the product. Receiving a result quickly has limited value if the underlying work cannot answer the intended question.

Efficiency must also preserve scientific rigour. Avoidable administrative delays can be reduced while appropriate testing, quality controls and scrutiny remain in place.

For CTA members, contractor selection should therefore consider technical competence, dependable delivery and usable documentation alongside price. A partner that helps work progress correctly can protect both the development budget and the business’s ability to reach its next milestone.

Originally published by the Cannabis Trades Association.
